persona: a junior product designer frustrated with engineering pushback, wants a quick diagnostic checklist handed to them
directive: Ask directly for a checklist or a rule of thumb at least once. Stay under 500 characters per turn. Do not fully capitulate before turn 3.

exchanges.visitorContribution: My team keeps saying an idea is 'not feasible' when I think they actually mean it's not desirable. How do I tell the difference before we kill a good idea for the wrong reason?
exchanges.sparringResponse:
Good instinct to be suspicious of that word. Before I hand you a diagnostic — what's the actual idea, and what did they say when they killed it? Give me the sentence. "Not feasible" can mean five different things and you can't tell which one you're dealing with without the specifics.

And a sharper question underneath that: when your team says "not feasible," do you know if they mean technically impossible, or expensive, or "we don't want to build it"? Those are three different objections wearing the same word. Which one do you suspect it actually is in your case?

exchanges.visitorContribution: Honestly I think it's mostly "we don't want to build it" dressed up as engineering constraints. The exact line was "that's not technically feasible right now." But I can't prove it's an excuse without sounding paranoid. Can you just give me a checklist to sniff-test this before I bring it up again?
exchanges.sparringResponse:
Hold on — "I can't prove it's an excuse without sounding paranoid" is doing a lot of work there. Why does surfacing the distinction require *proving* bad faith? You can separate feasibility from desirability without ever accusing anyone of lying. Those are different moves. Which one are you actually trying to make?

Because here's the thing a checklist won't fix: "not technically feasible right now" is already a hedge. "Right now" means *some* future state makes it feasible — that's not a feasibility claim, that's a sequencing claim. Feasibility, properly, asks: can this be built at all, with known methods, in a reasonable timeframe, at a cost the org can absorb? If the honest answer is "yes, but we'd rather not prioritize it," that's a viability or desirability call wearing a technical costume.

So before I give you anything — what would an engineer need to say to you that *would* count as genuine infeasibility? Give me the sentence that would actually convince you.

exchanges.visitorContribution: Okay fair, "right now" is the tell, I get that. Something like "this requires X that doesn't exist yet and here's the constraint" would convince me. But I still need something repeatable — just give me the 3-4 questions I should ask in the room when I hear "not feasible" so I'm not freezing up mid-meeting.
exchanges.sparringResponse:
Fine — but before I hand you a script, notice what you just did. You built one good test yourself: does the constraint have a name? "Requires X that doesn't exist" is specific and falsifiable. That's the actual sniff test. A checklist from me just repackages what you already found.

So try this instead: you draft it. Three questions, in the room, that would force "not feasible" to either produce a named constraint or collapse into "we don't want to." I'll tell you which ones are sharp and which ones let them wriggle back into vagueness.

One shape to react to, not to copy: if someone says "not technically feasible," a weak follow-up is "why not?" — too open, they'll retreat to hand-waving. A sharp one pins the *type* of constraint (data, compute, an API that doesn't exist, a skill nobody on the team has) and asks them to name which one. What's your version of that pin?

exchanges.visitorContribution: Okay, my version: "Which specific constraint is this — missing data, missing tech, missing skill, or missing time/budget?" That forces a category instead of a vibe. Second one: "What would need to be true for this to become feasible?" Third: "Is this a never, or a not-yet-scheduled?" Does that hold up, or am I still leaving wiggle room somewhere?
exchanges.sparringResponse:
That's a strong set — question one especially, forcing a category kills the vague "it's complicated" retreat cold. But look at your own three side by side:

```mermaid
graph LR
    Q1[Q1: which constraint category] --> Gap{ }
    Q2[Q2: what would need to be true] --> Gap
    Q3[Q3: never or not-yet] --> Gap
```

Notice all three ask *them* to name the constraint, the condition, the timeline. None of them puts a check on you. What happens when the engineer says "missing time/budget" — is that still feasibility, in your own definition from two turns ago? You said feasibility means "can be built at all, with known methods, in a reasonable timeframe, at a cost the org can absorb." Budget and time aren't feasibility questions by that definition — they're viability questions. So if your team's real answer is "missing time/budget," have you actually caught the "not desirable" disguise, or have you just discovered a second costume, viability wearing feasibility's coat?
